  echo stripslashes(json_encode($response));
} catch (Exception $e) {
  http_response_code(404);
}
```

## delete ($src)

Method used to delete an image from disk.

### **Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `$src` | String | The path relative to the `$_SERVER['DOCUMENT_ROOT']` global variable to the image that should be deleted. |

## getList ($folderPath, $thumbPath)

Method used to list all images from disk.

### **Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `$folderPath` | String | The path relative to the `$_SERVER['DOCUMENT_ROOT']` global variable from where the images are being loaded. |
| `$thumbPath` | String | The path relative to the `$_SERVER['DOCUMENT_ROOT']` global variable from where the image thumbs are being loaded. This parameter is optional, and defaults to `$folderPath`. |

### **Response**

If the request is completed successfully, the method returns an array with images. If an error occurs, the method throws an exception.

```php
try {
  $response = FroalaEditor_Image::getList('/uploads/');
  echo stripslashes(json_encode($response));
} catch (Exception $e) {
  http_response_code(404);
}
```

pages.markdown:
# Python SDK

The Python SDK handles the server side of the editor's uploads. It stores and deletes images and files, lists images for the image manager, resizes and validates uploads, and signs uploads that go straight to Amazon S3. Its source is on [GitHub](https://github.com/froala/wysiwyg-editor-python-sdk).

The SDK's code hasn't changed since April 2019. Its releases since then, the latest tagged on 30 September 2026, only move the editor version its demo page loads.

Its README still names Python 2, which went out of support in January 2020, and its Django example calls `render_to_response` and `url()`, which current Django no longer has. Test the SDK on your stack before you rely on it.

## About

The SDK reads uploads through an adapter for your framework. It ships three, and the repository has an example app for each.

| Framework | Adapter | Example app |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Django | `DjangoAdapter` | [django_examples](https://github.com/froala/wysiwyg-editor-python-sdk/tree/master/django_examples) |
| Flask | `FlaskAdapter` | [flask_examples](https://github.com/froala/wysiwyg-editor-python-sdk/tree/master/flask_examples) |
| Pyramid | `PyramidAdapter` | [pyramid_examples](https://github.com/froala/wysiwyg-editor-python-sdk/tree/master/pyramid_examples) |

For another framework, write your own adapter, as [Image Server Upload](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/sdks/python/image-server-upload/#custom-adapter) shows.

To put the editor in a Django form or model field, use the separate `django-froala-editor` package, which the [Django guide](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/framework-plugins/django/) covers.

## Download

The SDK isn't on PyPI. Clone the repository, or [download it as a zip](https://github.com/froala/wysiwyg-editor-python-sdk/archive/master.zip), and copy its `froala_editor` folder into your project.

```shell
git clone https://github.com/froala/wysiwyg-editor-python-sdk.git
cp -r wysiwyg-editor-python-sdk/froala_editor path/to/your/project/
```

The SDK needs Wand, the Python binding for ImageMagick, for every upload, files included, because it loads Wand as soon as you import it. Install Wand with pip and ImageMagick with your system's package manager.

```shell
pip install Wand
```

The current Wand release needs Python 3.8 or later.

[Wand installation guide](https://docs.wand-py.org/en/latest/guide/install.html)

## Import the SDK in Your App

```python
from froala_editor import File, Image, S3
from froala_editor import DjangoAdapter, FlaskAdapter, PyramidAdapter
# Or write your own adapter on froala_editor.adapters.BaseAdapter.
```

### Where Files Go

The paths you pass, such as `'/public/'`, are joined to the folder of the script that started the Python process (`sys.argv[0]`), not to your project. With `python manage.py runserver` that is your project. When a launcher such as `gunicorn` or `python -m flask run` starts the process, it is the launcher's own folder. To keep uploads in your project, set the folder once at startup.

```python
import os
from froala_editor.utils import Utils

# Uploads now go under this file's folder, however the server starts.
BASE_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
Utils.getServerPath = staticmethod(lambda: BASE_DIR)
```

## Additional Resources

- [Integrate Froala to Django Web Application with Image Upload](https://froala.com/blog/general/integrate-froala-to-django-web-application-with-image-upload/)
- [Easily Upload Images To Your Server With Python Flask](https://froala.com/blog/general/easily-upload-images-to-your-server-with-python-flask/)
- [What’s The Best Django WYSIWYG Editor With Image Upload?](https://froala.com/blog/editor/whats-the-best-django-wysiwyg-editor-with-image-upload/)

pages.markdown:
# Python File S3 Upload

## How it works

1. Create a bucket on Amazon S3 and set the CORS for it.
2. Code computes the Amazon S3 signature on server side.
3. The editor initializes with the `fileUploadToS3` option.
4. Uploaded files go directly to the S3 bucket without passing through the server.

[Jump to Complete Example](#complete-example)

## Create a S3 Bucket

For information on creating a bucket and setting a region, refer to the [Amazon documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/create-bucket-overview.html). If you have any issues creating it, please [contact Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/contact-us/) for getting it set up.

A new bucket has ACLs turned off and doesn't allow public access, so S3 refuses an upload whose `acl` is `public-read`. Either allow ACLs and public ACLs on the bucket, or set `acl` to `bucket-owner-full-control` and make the folder readable another way, such as a [bucket policy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/example-bucket-policies.html).

## Set CORS on the S3 Bucket

Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) tells Amazon from which domains to accept requests and what kind of requests. For a detailed explanation of how that works, refer to the [Amazon CORS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/cors.html).

The following example shows the recommended configuration, remember to replace `ALLOWED_URL` with the URL of the page where you are using editor.

```json
[
  {
    "AllowedOrigins": ["ALLOWED_URL"],
    "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "POST", "PUT"],
    "AllowedHeaders": ["*"],
    "MaxAgeSeconds": 3000
  }
]
```

## Compute Signature

To get the file uploaded to S3, it is necessary to compute a signature using the `AWS access key ID` and `AWS secret access key` and provide it together with the upload request. The editor Python SDK comes with methods to compute the S3 signature using the V4 signing algorithm that works with buckets created on any of the S3 regions.

```python
config = {
    # The name of your bucket.
    'bucket': 'bucket-name',

    # S3 region. If you are using the default us-east-1, it this can be ignored.
    'region': 'eu-west-1',

    # The folder where to upload the file.
    'keyStart': 'uploads/',

    # File access.
    'acl': 'public-read',

    # AWS keys.
    'accessKey': YOUR_AWS_ACCESS_KEY,
    'secretKey': YOUR_AWS_SECRET_KEY
}

s3Hash = S3.getHash(config)
```

`S3.getHash` returns the region as `s3-<region>`, and the editor uploads to `https://s3-<region>.amazonaws.com/<bucket>`. Only [some older regions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/VirtualHosting.html) have that address. For a newer region, add `uploadURL` to the hash, which the editor uses in place of the bucket and region, for example `s3Hash['uploadURL'] = 'https://bucket-name.s3.eu-south-1.amazonaws.com'`.

## Initialize the javascript editor

To upload files to Amazon S3, set the `fileUploadToS3` option on initialization. The [editor Python SDK computes the hash](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/sdks/python/references/s3/) required for this as the response of the `S3.getHash` method.

```html
<script>
  fetch('/get_signature')
    .then(function (response) { return response.json(); })
    .then(function (s3Hash) {
      new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
        fileUploadToS3: s3Hash
      });
    });
</script>
```

## Complete Example

```json
[
  {
    "AllowedOrigins": ["ALLOWED_URL"],
    "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "POST", "PUT"],
    "AllowedHeaders": ["*"],
    "MaxAgeSeconds": 3000
  }
]
```

```python
# Django
from django.http import HttpResponse
import json
import sys
from froala_editor import S3

def get_signature(request):
    config = {
        # The name of your bucket.
        'bucket': 'bucket-name',

        # S3 region. If you are using the default us-east-1, it this can be ignored.
        'region': 'eu-west-1',

        # The folder where to upload the files.
        'keyStart': 'uploads/',

        # File access.
        'acl': 'public-read',

        # AWS keys.
        'accessKey': YOUR_AWS_ACCESS_KEY,
        'secretKey': YOUR_AWS_SECRET_KEY
    }
    try:
        response = S3.getHash(config)
    except Exception:
        response = {'error': str(sys.exc_info()[1])}
    return HttpResponse(json.dumps(response), content_type="application/json")
```

```python
# Flask
import sys
from flask import jsonify
from froala_editor import S3

@app.route('/get_signature')
def get_signature():
    config = {
        # The name of your bucket.
        'bucket': 'bucket-name',

        # S3 region. If you are using the default us-east-1, it this can be ignored.
        'region': 'eu-west-1',

        # The folder where to upload the files.
        'keyStart': 'uploads/',

        # File access.
        'acl': 'public-read',

        # AWS keys.
        'accessKey': YOUR_AWS_ACCESS_KEY,
        'secretKey': YOUR_AWS_SECRET_KEY
    }
    try:
        response = S3.getHash(config)
    except Exception:
        response = {'error': str(sys.exc_info()[1])}
    return jsonify(**response)
```

```python

    config = {
        # The name of your bucket.
        'bucket': 'bucket-name',

        'region': 'eu-west-1',

        # The folder where to upload the files.
        'keyStart': 'uploads/',

        # File access.
        'acl': 'public-read',

        # AWS keys.
        'accessKey': YOUR_AWS_ACCESS_KEY,
        'secretKey': YOUR_AWS_SECRET_KEY
    }

        response = S3.getHash(config)

    return response

      });

</script>
```

# Python File Server Upload

## How it works

1. Specify upload options when initializing the editor.
2. On file insertion, the editor automatically makes an AJAX request to the server.
3. Once the request reaches the server, it stores the file and sends back to the client the link to the uploaded file.

[Jump to Complete Example](#complete-example)

## Initialize the editor

First, set the `fileUploadURL` option and specify the URL destination for the uploaded files.

Next, set any additional options to configure upload methods and allowed file types. `fileUploadParam`, `fileUploadParams`, `fileUploadMethod`, `fileMaxSize`, `fileAllowedTypes`.

```html
<script>
  new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
    // Set the file upload URL.
    fileUploadURL: '/upload_file'
  })
</script>
```

## Receive the uploaded file and store it

The server implementation is responsible for receiving the request and handling it appropriately. In Python, the uploaded file is available in the `request` received by your application. However you should wrap the `request` object into an adapter. The Python SDK contains 3 adapters (Django, Flask and Pyramid) and you can create your custom adapter by implementing `BaseAdapter` class.

```python
# Django adapter example.

from froala_editor.adapters import BaseAdapter

class DjangoAdapter(BaseAdapter):
    """
    Django Adapter: Check BaseAdapter to see what methods description.
    """

    def checkFile(self, fieldname):
        if fieldname not in self.request.FILES:
            raise Exception("File does not exist.")

    def getFilename(self, fieldname):
        self.checkFile(fieldname)
        return self.request.FILES[fieldname].name

    def getMimetype(self, fieldname):
        self.checkFile(fieldname)
        return self.request.FILES[fieldname].content_type

    def saveFile(self, fieldname, fullNamePath):
        self.checkFile(fieldname)

        with open(fullNamePath, 'wb+') as destination:
            for chunk in self.request.FILES[fieldname].chunks():
                destination.write(chunk)
```

You should override all methods from BaseAdapter. The Python editor SDK detects the uploaded file automatically but you have to specify the path where to store it.

The SDK joins the path to the folder of the script that started the server, as [Where Files Go](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/sdks/python/#where-files-go) explains.

```python
from froala_editor import File, FlaskAdapter

response = File.upload(FlaskAdapter(request), '/public/')
```

The editor sends files of any type by default, but the SDK's default validation allows only TXT, PDF and DOC files, so it rejects the rest. To accept other types, set them as [File Validation](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/sdks/python/file-validation/) shows.

To store the uploaded file, the server needs write rights on the uploads folder. Additionally, check uploaded files are publicly accessible in the browser.

## Return the path to the uploaded file

If the save action is successful, `File.upload` returns a dictionary with the link to the uploaded file, such as `{'link': '/public/3f2a9c.pdf'}`, and the server returns it to the client side.

```python
# Return a json. You can use json.dumps to transform the response dictionary into a json string.
json.dumps(response)
```

## Complete Example

```html
<script>
  new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
    // Set the file upload URL.
    fileUploadURL: '/upload_file'
  })
</script>
```

```python
# Django
from django.http import HttpResponse
import json
import sys
from froala_editor import File
from froala_editor import DjangoAdapter

def upload_file(request):
    try:
        response = File.upload(DjangoAdapter(request), '/public/')
    except Exception:
        response = {'error': str(sys.exc_info()[1])}
    return HttpResponse(json.dumps(response), content_type="application/json")
```

Django rejects a POST without its CSRF token. Send the token with the editor's `requestHeaders` option, for example `requestHeaders: { 'X-CSRFToken': '{{ csrf_token }}' }` in a Django template.

```python
# Flask
from flask import request
import json
import sys
from froala_editor import File
from froala_editor import FlaskAdapter

@app.route('/upload_file', methods=['POST'])
def upload_file():
    try:
        response = File.upload(FlaskAdapter(request), '/public/')
    except Exception:
        response = {'error': str(sys.exc_info()[1])}
    return json.dumps(response)
```

```python
# Pyramid
from pyramid.response import Response
import json
import sys
from froala_editor import File
from froala_editor import PyramidAdapter

def upload_file(request):
    try:
        response = File.upload(PyramidAdapter(request), '/public/')
    except Exception:
        response = {'error': str(sys.exc_info()[1])}
    return Response(json.dumps(response))
```

- [Easily Upload Images To Your Server With Python Flask](https://froala.com/blog/general/easily-upload-images-to-your-server-with-python-flask/)
- [What’s The Best Django WYSIWYG Editor With Image Upload?](https://froala.com/blog/editor/whats-the-best-django-wysiwyg-editor-with-image-upload/)

pages.markdown:
# Python Image Server Upload

Store the images users insert in the editor on your own server with `Image.upload` from the Python SDK.

## How It Works

1. You set the upload options when you start the editor.
2. When a user inserts an image, the editor sends it to your server.
3. The server stores the image and replies with its link, which the editor puts in the content.

## Initialize the Editor

Set `imageUploadURL` to the route that receives the images.

```js
new FroalaEditor('#editor', {
  imageUploadURL: '/upload_image'
});
```

These options shape the request, and what the editor accepts before it sends anything.

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`imageUploadParam`](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/options/#imageUploadParam) | `'file'` | The name of the field that holds the image. The SDK reads `file` unless you pass another `fieldname`. |
| [`imageUploadParams`](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/options/#imageUploadParams) | `{}` | Extra fields sent with the image. |
| [`imageUploadMethod`](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/options/#imageUploadMethod) | `'POST'` | The HTTP method of the request. |
| [`imageMaxSize`](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/options/#imageMaxSize) | `1024 * 1024 * 10` | The largest image the editor sends, in bytes. |
| [`imageAllowedTypes`](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/options/#imageAllowedTypes) | `['jpeg', 'jpg', 'png', 'gif', 'webp']` | The image types the editor sends. |

Django rejects a POST without its CSRF token. Send the token with the editor's `requestHeaders` option, for example `requestHeaders: { 'X-CSRFToken': '{{ csrf_token }}' }` in a Django template.

## Receive the Uploaded Image and Store It

Wrap your framework's request in its adapter and pass it to `Image.upload` with the folder to store the image in. The SDK finds the image in the request, saves it under a new random name and keeps its extension.

```python
from froala_editor import Image, FlaskAdapter

response = Image.upload(FlaskAdapter(request), '/public/')
```

The folder path starts and ends with a slash. The SDK joins it to the folder of the script that started the server, as [Where Files Go](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/sdks/python/#where-files-go) explains. It doesn't create the folder, so make it first and give the server write access to it.

The editor sends WebP images by default, but the SDK's default validation allows only GIF, JPEG, PNG and SVG, so it rejects them. To accept WebP, add it as [Image Validation](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/sdks/python/image-validation/) shows.

### Custom Adapter

For a framework without an adapter, subclass `BaseAdapter` and implement its three methods. The SDK calls each with the field name, and `self.request` is the request you passed in. This is the Django adapter the SDK ships.

```python
from froala_editor.adapters import BaseAdapter

class DjangoAdapter(BaseAdapter):

    def checkFile(self, fieldname):
        if fieldname not in self.request.FILES:
            raise Exception("File does not exist.")

    # The name of the uploaded file.
    def getFilename(self, fieldname):
        self.checkFile(fieldname)
        return self.request.FILES[fieldname].name

    # Its MIME type, as the browser sent it.
    def getMimetype(self, fieldname):
        self.checkFile(fieldname)
        return self.request.FILES[fieldname].content_type

    # Write it to fullNamePath.
    def saveFile(self, fieldname, fullNamePath):
        self.checkFile(fieldname)
        with open(fullNamePath, 'wb+') as destination:
            for chunk in self.request.FILES[fieldname].chunks():
                destination.write(chunk)
```

## Return the Path to the Uploaded Image

`Image.upload` returns a dictionary with the image's link, the folder path and the new name, such as `{'link': '/public/3f2a9c.jpg'}`. Send it back as JSON. The editor loads the image from that link, so serve the folder at the same path.

```python
return json.dumps(response)
```

When the upload fails, `Image.upload` raises an exception. Reply with JSON that has no `link`, such as `{'error': 'File does not meet the validation.'}`, and the editor fires [`image.error`](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/events/#image.error) instead of inserting the image.

## Complete Example

```js
new FroalaEditor('#editor', {
  imageUploadURL: '/upload_image'
});
```

**Django**

```python
# views.py
from django.http import JsonResponse
from froala_editor import Image, DjangoAdapter

def upload_image(request):
    try:
        response = Image.upload(DjangoAdapter(request), '/public/')
    except Exception as e:
        response = {'error': str(e)}
    return JsonResponse(response)

# urls.py
# path('upload_image', views.upload_image)
```

**Flask**

```python
import json
from flask import Flask, request
from froala_editor import Image, FlaskAdapter

# Serves the public folder at /public, where the links point.
app = Flask(__name__, static_folder='public', static_url_path='/public')

@app.route('/upload_image', methods=['POST'])
def upload_image():
    try:
        response = Image.upload(FlaskAdapter(request), '/public/')
    except Exception as e:
        response = {'error': str(e)}
    return json.dumps(response)
```

**Pyramid**

```python
from froala_editor import Image, PyramidAdapter

def upload_image(request):
    try:
        return Image.upload(PyramidAdapter(request), '/public/')
    except Exception as e:
        return {'error': str(e)}

# config.add_route('upload_image', '/upload_image')
# config.add_view(upload_image, route_name='upload_image', renderer='json')
# config.add_static_view('public', path='public/')
```

Returns a dictionary.

Method used to upload file to the specified location on disk.

### **Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `req` | Request Object that implements BaseAdapter interface | The Python SDK contains 3 adapters (Django, Flask and Pyramid) and you can create your custom adapter by implementing `BaseAdapter` class. |
| `fileRoute` | String | The server route where the file will be uploaded. This route must be public to be accessed by the editor. |
| `options` | Dictionary | This parameter is optional. It can be used to pass custom options for the file upload. |

```python
# Django adapter example.

from froala_editor.adapters import BaseAdapter

class DjangoAdapter(BaseAdapter):
    """
    Django Adapter: Check BaseAdapter to see what methods description.
    """

    def checkFile(self, fieldname):
        if fieldname not in self.request.FILES:
            raise Exception("File does not exist.")

    def getFilename(self, fieldname):
        self.checkFile(fieldname)
        return self.request.FILES[fieldname].name

    def getMimetype(self, fieldname):
        self.checkFile(fieldname)
        return self.request.FILES[fieldname].content_type

    def saveFile(self, fieldname, fullNamePath):
        self.checkFile(fieldname)

        with open(fullNamePath, 'wb+') as destination:
            for chunk in self.request.FILES[fieldname].chunks():
                destination.write(chunk)
```

You should override all methods from BaseAdapter.

### **options parameter**

- **fieldname** The field name from the request object.  Type.StringDefault.'file'
- **validation** A dictionary or a function used to validate the uploaded file. The dictionary specifies the allowed file extensions through `allowedExts` and the allowed mime types through `allowedMimeTypes`. The function is invoked with `filePath` and `mimetype`.  Type.Dictionary or FunctionDefault.{ 'allowedExts': ['txt', 'pdf', 'doc'], 'allowedMimeTypes': ['text/plain', 'application/msword', 'application/x-pdf', 'application/pdf'] }

### **Response**

If the upload is completed successfully, the method returns a dictionary with the link to the uploaded file, such as `{'link': '/public/3f2a9c.pdf'}`. If an error occurs, the method throws an exception.

```python
try:
    response = File.upload(DjangoAdapter(request), '/public/')
except Exception:
    response = {'error': str(sys.exc_info()[1])}

return HttpResponse(json.dumps(response), content_type="application/json")
```

## delete (src)

Method used to delete a file from disk. It doesn't raise an error when the file is missing or can't be deleted.

### **Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src` | String | The file path available in the body of the request under `src` key. |

pages.markdown:
# Ruby File S3 Upload

## How it works

1. Create a bucket on Amazon S3 and set the CORS for it.
2. Code computes the Amazon S3 signature on server side.
3. The editor initializes with the `fileUploadToS3` option.
4. Uploaded files go directly to the S3 bucket without passing through the server.

[Jump to Complete Example](#complete-example)

## Create a S3 Bucket

For information on creating a bucket and setting a region, refer to the [Amazon documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/create-bucket-overview.html). If you have any issues creating it, please [contact Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/contact-us/) for getting it set up.

A new bucket has ACLs turned off and blocks public access, so S3 refuses an upload whose `acl` is `public-read`. Either allow ACLs and public ACLs on the bucket, or set `acl` to `bucket-owner-full-control` and make the folder readable another way, such as a [bucket policy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/example-bucket-policies.html).

## Set CORS on the S3 Bucket

Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) tells Amazon from which domains to accept requests and what kind of requests. For a detailed explanation of how that works, refer to the [Amazon CORS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/cors.html).

The following example shows the recomended configuration, remember to replace `ALLOWED_URL` with the URL of the page where you are using editor.

```json
[
  {
    "AllowedOrigins": ["ALLOWED_URL"],
    "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "POST", "PUT"],
    "MaxAgeSeconds": 3000,
    "AllowedHeaders": ["*"]
  }
]
```

The S3 console takes the rule as JSON only. The S3 API also takes it as XML.

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<CORSConfiguration xmlns="http://s3.amazonaws.com/doc/2006-03-01/">
  <CORSRule>
    <AllowedOrigin>ALLOWED_URL</AllowedOrigin>
    <AllowedMethod>GET</AllowedMethod>
    <AllowedMethod>POST</AllowedMethod>
    <AllowedMethod>PUT</AllowedMethod>
    <MaxAgeSeconds>3000</MaxAgeSeconds>
    <AllowedHeader>*</AllowedHeader>
  </CORSRule>
</CORSConfiguration>
```

## Compute Signature

To get the file uploaded to S3, it is necessary to compute a signature using the `AWS access key ID` and `AWS secret access key` and provide it together with the upload request. The editor Ruby SDK comes with methods to compute the S3 signature using the V4 signing algorithm that works with buckets created on any of the S3 regions.

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def index
    # Configuration object.
    options = {
      # The name of your bucket.
      bucket: 'bucket-name',

      # S3 region. If you are using the default us-east-1, it this can be ignored.
      region: 'eu-west-1',

      # The folder where to upload the files.
      keyStart: 'uploads/',

      # File access.
      acl: 'public-read',

      # AWS keys.
      accessKey: 'YOUR_AWS_ACCESS_KEY',
      secretKey: 'YOUR_AWS_SECRET_KEY'
    }

    # Compute the signature.
    @aws_data = FroalaEditorSDK::S3.data_hash(options)
  end

  ...

end
```

`data_hash` returns the region as `s3-<region>`, and the editor uploads to `https://s3-<region>.amazonaws.com/<bucket>`. Only some older regions have that address. For a newer region, add an `uploadURL` to the hash, which the editor uses in place of the bucket and region, such as `@aws_data[:uploadURL] = 'https://s3.eu-south-1.amazonaws.com/bucket-name'`.

## Initialize the javascript editor

To upload files to Amazon S3, set the `fileUploadToS3` option on initialization. The editor Ruby SDK computes the hash required for this as the response of the `FroalaEditorSDK::S3.data_hash` method.

```html
<script>
  new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
    fileUploadToS3: <%= @aws_data.to_json.html_safe %>
  })
</script>
```

## Complete Example

```html
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<CORSConfiguration xmlns="http://s3.amazonaws.com/doc/2006-03-01/">
  <CORSRule>
    <AllowedOrigin>ALLOWED_URL</AllowedOrigin>
    <AllowedMethod>GET</AllowedMethod>
    <AllowedMethod>POST</AllowedMethod>
    <AllowedMethod>PUT</AllowedMethod>
    <MaxAgeSeconds>3000</MaxAgeSeconds>
    <AllowedHeader>*</AllowedHeader>
  </CORSRule>
</CORSConfiguration>
```

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def index
    options = {
      # The name of your bucket.
      bucket: 'bucket-name',

      # S3 region. If you are using the default us-east-1, it this can be ignored.
      region: 'eu-west-1',

      # The folder where to upload the files.
      keyStart: 'uploads/',

      # File access.
      acl: 'public-read',

      # AWS keys.
      accessKey: 'YOUR_AWS_ACCESS_KEY',
      secretKey: 'YOUR_AWS_SECRET_KEY'
    }
    @aws_data = FroalaEditorSDK::S3.data_hash(options)
  end

  ...

end
```

The view.

```html
<script>
  new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
    fileUploadToS3: <%= @aws_data.to_json.html_safe %>
  })
</script>
```

# Ruby File Server Upload

## How it works

1. Specify upload options when initializing the editor.
2. On file insertion, the editor automatically makes an AJAX request to the server.
3. Once the request reaches the server, it stores the file and sends back to the client the link to the uploaded file.

[Jump to Complete Example](#complete-example)

## Initialize the editor

First, set the `fileUploadURL` option and specify the URL destination for the uploaded files.

Next, set any additional options to configure upload methods and allowed file types. `fileUploadParam`, `fileUploadParams`, `fileUploadMethod`, `fileMaxSize`, `fileAllowedTypes`.

```html
<script>
  new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
    // Set the file upload URL.
    fileUploadURL: '/upload_file'
  })
</script>
```

A controller that inherits from `ActionController::Base` rejects a POST without the CSRF token. Send the token with the editor's `requestHeaders` option, for example `requestHeaders: { 'X-CSRF-Token': document.querySelector('meta[name="csrf-token"]').content }`, which reads the tag `csrf_meta_tags` puts in your layout.

## Receive the uploaded file and store it

The server implementation is responsible for receiving the request and handling it appropriately. In Ruby, the uploaded file is available in the `params` global variable. The Ruby editor SDK detects the uploaded file automatically but you have to specify the path where to store it.

The path of the file is relative to the `Rails.root` global variable.

```ruby
FroalaEditorSDK::File.upload(params, "public/uploads/files/", { file_access_path: '/uploads/files/' })
```

To store the uploaded file, the server needs write rights on the uploads folder. Additionally, check uploaded files are publicly accessible in the browser.

## Return the path to the uploaded file

If the save action is successful, the SDK returns JSON with the link to the uploaded file, such as `{"link":"/uploads/files/abc.pdf"}`, and the server returns it to the client side. The link is the `file_access_path` option followed by the new file name. That option is `/uploads/` unless you set it, so set it to the address where the folder is served.

```ruby
render :json => FroalaEditorSDK::File.upload(params, "public/uploads/files/", { file_access_path: '/uploads/files/' })
```

## Complete Example

```html
<script>
  new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
    // Set the file upload URL.
    fileUploadURL: '/upload_file'
  })
</script>
```

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def upload_file
    render :json => FroalaEditorSDK::File.upload(params, "public/uploads/files/", { file_access_path: '/uploads/files/' })
  end

  ...

end
```

pages.markdown:
# Ruby File Validation

## How it works

1. The file gets uploaded to your server.
2. Before storing the file on disk, it is being validated on server side.

[Jump to Complete Example](#complete-example)

## File Upload

In the [Server Upload](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/sdks/ruby/file-server-upload/) article we explain the steps to upload an file on your server. When you insert an file in the rich text editor, you can validate its format. However that check is done only on the filename and not on the mime type. We recommend to make additional checks on server side just to make sure that users don't upload files in bad formats.

## Validate Extension

The WYSIWYG editor's Ruby SDK comes with the possibility to [check the file extension](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/sdks/ruby/references/file/) when it is being stored on the disk. It also takes a list of allowed mime types, but the current gem never checks that list, so check the type in a custom validation if you need to.

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def upload_file
    options = {
      fieldname: 'file',
      validation: {
        allowedExts: [".txt", ".pdf", ".doc", ".json", ".html"],
        allowedMimeTypes: [ "text/plain", "application/msword", "application/x-pdf", "application/pdf", "application/json","text/html" ]
      },
      file_access_path: '/uploads/files/'
    }

    # Upload the file.
    render :json => FroalaEditorSDK::File.upload(params, "public/uploads/files/", options)
  end

  ...

end
```

## Custom Validation

You can also pass a custom method instead of validating the extension and mime type. This gives you full control on what types of files you want to store on disk. Below is an example of how to validate if a file is smaller than 10Mb.

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def upload_file
    options = {
      validation: Proc.new do |file, type|
        if File.size(file) > 10 * 1024 * 1024
          raise 'File size exceeded'
        end
      end,
      file_access_path: '/uploads/files/'
    }
    render :json => FroalaEditorSDK::File.upload(params, "public/uploads/files/", options)
  end

  ...

end
```

</script>

# Ruby Image Manager

## How it works

1. Specify image load options when the editor is initialized on the client side.
2. When the Image Manger modal displays, the editor makes a request to the server to load the images.
3. Once the request reaches the server, it returns a list with the images to display in the editor.
4. The editor processes the server response and renders the images in its interface.

[Jump to Complete Example](#complete-example)

## Initialize the editor

First, set the `imageManagerLoadURL` and `imageManagerDeleteURL` options, this allows the editor to interact with the server to load and delete images listed on the Image Manager.

Next, you can set other options related to the interaction between the server and the editor. `imageManagerLoadMethod`, `imageManagerLoadParams`, `imageManagerPreloader`, `imageManagerDeleteParams`.

```html
<script>
  new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
    // Set the image load URL.
    imageManagerLoadURL: '/load_images',

    // Set the image delete URL.
    imageManagerDeleteURL: '/delete_image'
  })
</script>
```

The editor loads the images with a GET request and deletes them with a POST. A controller that inherits from `ActionController::Base` rejects a POST without the CSRF token. Send the token with the editor's `requestHeaders` option, for example `requestHeaders: { 'X-CSRF-Token': document.querySelector('meta[name="csrf-token"]').content }`, which reads the tag `csrf_meta_tags` puts in your layout.

## Receive the load request

The server implementation is responsible for receiving the request and handling it appropriately. The Ruby SDK can load all the images inside a specified folder using the `FroalaEditorSDK::Image.load_images` method. Each image's link is the `file_access_path` option followed by its file name, so pass the same `file_access_path` as for uploads.

The path of the folder from where the images are being loaded is relative to the `Rails.root` global variable.

```ruby
FroalaEditorSDK::Image.load_images("public/uploads/images/", { file_access_path: '/uploads/images/' })
```

## Receive the delete request

The server should listen for any delete request and process it accordingly. The initialization step makes the image path available in the `params[:src]` variable. The `FroalaEditorSDK::Image.delete()` method from the Ruby SDK expects the path of the image and the folder to remove it from.

```ruby
FroalaEditorSDK::Image.delete(params[:src], "public/uploads/images/")
```

## Complete Example

```html
<script>
  new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
    // Set the image load URL.
    imageManagerLoadURL: '/load_images',

    // Set the image delete URL.
    imageManagerDeleteURL: '/delete_image'
  })
</script>
```

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def load_images
    render :json => FroalaEditorSDK::Image.load_images("public/uploads/images/", { file_access_path: '/uploads/images/' })
  end

  ...

end
```

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def delete_image
    render :json => FroalaEditorSDK::Image.delete(params[:src], "public/uploads/images/")
  end

  ...

end
```

class UploadController < ActionController::Base

pages.title: Ruby Image S3 Upload
headings: Set CORS on the S3 Bucket
pages.markdown:
# Ruby Image S3 Upload

## How it works

1. Create a bucket on Amazon S3 and set the CORS for it.
2. Code computes the Amazon S3 signature on the server side.
3. The editor initializes with the `imageUploadToS3` option.
4. Uploaded images go directly to the S3 bucket without passing through the server.

[Jump to Complete Example](#complete-example)

## Create a S3 Bucket

For information on creating a bucket and setting a region, refer to the [Amazon documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/create-bucket-overview.html). If you have any issues creating it, please [contact Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/contact-us/) for getting it set up.

A new bucket has ACLs turned off and blocks public access, so S3 refuses an upload whose `acl` is `public-read`. Either allow ACLs and public ACLs on the bucket, or set `acl` to `bucket-owner-full-control` and make the folder readable another way, such as a [bucket policy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/example-bucket-policies.html).

## Set CORS on the S3 Bucket

Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) tells Amazon from which domains to accept requests and what kind of requests. For a detailed explanation of how that works, refer to the [Amazon CORS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/cors.html).

The following example shows the recomended configuration, remember to replace `ALLOWED_URL` with the URL of the page where you are using editor.

```json
[
  {
    "AllowedOrigins": ["ALLOWED_URL"],
    "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "POST", "PUT"],
    "MaxAgeSeconds": 3000,
    "AllowedHeaders": ["*"]
  }
]
```

The S3 console takes the rule as JSON only. The S3 API also takes it as XML.

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<CORSConfiguration xmlns="http://s3.amazonaws.com/doc/2006-03-01/">
  <CORSRule>
    <AllowedOrigin>ALLOWED_URL</AllowedOrigin>
    <AllowedMethod>GET</AllowedMethod>
    <AllowedMethod>POST</AllowedMethod>
    <AllowedMethod>PUT</AllowedMethod>
    <MaxAgeSeconds>3000</MaxAgeSeconds>
    <AllowedHeader>*</AllowedHeader>
  </CORSRule>
</CORSConfiguration>
```

## Compute Signature

To send uploaded images to S3, it is necessary to compute a signature using the `AWS access key ID` and `AWS secret access key` and provide it together with the upload request. The editor Ruby SDK comes with methods to compute the S3 signature using the V4 signing algorithm that works with buckets created on any of the S3 regions.

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def index
    # Configuration object.
    options = {
      # The name of your bucket.
      bucket: 'bucket-name',

      # S3 region. If you are using the default us-east-1, it this can be ignored.
      region: 'eu-west-1',

      # The folder where to upload the images.
      keyStart: 'uploads/',

      # File access.
      acl: 'public-read',

      # AWS keys.
      accessKey: 'YOUR_AWS_ACCESS_KEY',
      secretKey: 'YOUR_AWS_SECRET_KEY'
    }

    # Compute the signature.
    @aws_data = FroalaEditorSDK::S3.data_hash(options)
  end

  ...

end
```

`data_hash` returns the region as `s3-<region>`, and the editor uploads to `https://s3-<region>.amazonaws.com/<bucket>`. Only some older regions have that address. For a newer region, add an `uploadURL` to the hash, which the editor uses in place of the bucket and region, such as `@aws_data[:uploadURL] = 'https://s3.eu-south-1.amazonaws.com/bucket-name'`.

## Initialize the Javascript editor

To upload images to Amazon S3, set the `imageUploadToS3` option on initialization. The editor Ruby SDK computes the hash required for this as the response of the `FroalaEditorSDK::S3.data_hash` method.

```html
<script>
  new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
    imageUploadToS3: <%= @aws_data.to_json.html_safe %>
  })
</script>
```

## Complete Example

```html
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<CORSConfiguration xmlns="http://s3.amazonaws.com/doc/2006-03-01/">
  <CORSRule>
    <AllowedOrigin>ALLOWED_URL</AllowedOrigin>
    <AllowedMethod>GET</AllowedMethod>
    <AllowedMethod>POST</AllowedMethod>
    <AllowedMethod>PUT</AllowedMethod>
    <MaxAgeSeconds>3000</MaxAgeSeconds>
    <AllowedHeader>*</AllowedHeader>
  </CORSRule>
</CORSConfiguration>
```

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def index
    options = {
      # The name of your bucket.
      bucket: 'bucket-name',

      # S3 region. If you are using the default us-east-1, it this can be ignored.
      region: 'eu-west-1',

      # The folder where to upload the images.
      keyStart: 'uploads/',

      # File access.
      acl: 'public-read',

      # AWS keys.
      accessKey: 'YOUR_AWS_ACCESS_KEY',
      secretKey: 'YOUR_AWS_SECRET_KEY'
    }

    # Compute the signature.
    @aws_data = FroalaEditorSDK::S3.data_hash(options)
  end

  ...

end
```

For the view.

```html
<script>
  new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
    imageUploadToS3: <%= @aws_data.to_json.html_safe %>
  })
</script>
```

# Ruby Image Server Upload

## How it works

1. Specify upload options when initializing the editor.
2. On image insertion, the editor automatically makes an AJAX request to the server.
3. Once the request reaches the server, it stores the image and sends back to the client the link to the uploaded image.

[Jump to Complete Example](#complete-example)

## Initialize the editor

First, add the `imageUploadURL` option, as its value enter the upload destination for the images.

Next, set any additional options to configure upload methods and allowed file types. `imageUploadParam`, `imageUploadParams`, `imageUploadMethod`, `imageMaxSize`, `imageAllowedTypes`.

```html
<script>
  new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
    // Set the image upload URL.
    imageUploadURL: '/upload_image'
  })
</script>
```

A controller that inherits from `ActionController::Base` rejects a POST without the CSRF token. Send the token with the editor's `requestHeaders` option, for example `requestHeaders: { 'X-CSRF-Token': document.querySelector('meta[name="csrf-token"]').content }`, which reads the tag `csrf_meta_tags` puts in your layout.

## Receive the uploaded image and store it

The server implementation is responsible for receiving the request and handling it appropriately. In Ruby, the uploaded image is available in the `params` global variable. The Ruby editor SDK detects the uploaded image automatically but you have to specify the path where to store it.

The path of the image is relative to the `Rails.root` global variable.

```ruby
FroalaEditorSDK::Image.upload(params, "public/uploads/images/", { file_access_path: '/uploads/images/' })
```

To store the uploaded image, the server needs write rights on the uploads folder. Additionally, check uploaded images are publicly accessible in the browser.

## Return the path to the uploaded image

If the save action is successful, the SDK returns JSON with the link to the uploaded image, such as `{"link":"/uploads/images/abc.jpg"}`, and the server returns it to the client side. The link is the `file_access_path` option followed by the new file name. That option is `/uploads/` unless you set it, so set it to the address where the folder is served.

```ruby
render :json => FroalaEditorSDK::Image.upload(params, "public/uploads/images/", { file_access_path: '/uploads/images/' })
```

## Complete Example

```html
<script>
  new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
    // Set the image upload URL.
    imageUploadURL: '/upload_image'
  })
</script>
```

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def upload_image
    render :json => FroalaEditorSDK::Image.upload(params, "public/uploads/images/", { file_access_path: '/uploads/images/' })
  end

  ...

end
```

pages.title: Ruby Image Validation
pages.markdown:
# Ruby Image Validation

## How it works

1. The image gets uploaded to your server.
2. Before storing the image on disk, it is being validated on server side.

[Jump to Complete Example](#complete-example)

## Image Upload

The [Server Upload](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/sdks/ruby/image-server-upload/) section describes the steps to upload an image to a server. You can validate images when you insert them in the editor, however that only checks the filename and not the mime type. It is advisable to make additional checks on the server side to make sure users only upload valid image formats.

## Validate Extension

The editor's Ruby SDK can check the image extension before storing it on disk. It also takes a list of allowed mime types, but the current gem never checks that list, so check the type in a custom validation if you need to.

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def image_upload
    options = {
      fieldname: 'file',
      validation: {
        allowedExts: [".gif", ".jpeg", ".jpg", ".png", ".svg", ".blob"],
        allowedMimeTypes: [ "image/gif", "image/jpeg", "image/pjpeg", "image/x-png", "image/png", "image/svg+xml" ]
      },
      file_access_path: '/uploads/images/'
    }

    # Store the image.
    render :json => FroalaEditorSDK::Image.upload(params, "public/uploads/images/", options)
  end

  ...

end
```

## Custom Validation

You can also pass a custom method instead of validating the extension and mime type. This gives you full control on what types of images you want to store on disk. Below is an example of how to validate if an image is square.

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def image_upload
    options = {
      validation: Proc.new do |file, type|
        img = MiniMagick::Image.open(file)
        if img.width != img.height
          raise 'Image is not square'
        end
      end,
      file_access_path: '/uploads/images/'
    }

    render :json => FroalaEditorSDK::Image.upload(params, "public/uploads/images/", options)
  end

  ...

end
```

## Complete Example

```html
<script>
  new FroalaEditor('.selector', {
    // Set the image upload URL.
    imageUploadURL: '/image_upload'
  })
</script>
```

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def upload_file_validation
    options = {
      validation: Proc.new do |file, type|
        img = MiniMagick::Image.open(file)
        if img.width != img.height
          raise 'Image is not square'
        end
      end,
      file_access_path: '/uploads/images/'
    }

    render :json => FroalaEditorSDK::Image.upload(params, "public/uploads/images/", options)
  end

  ...

end
```

pages.title: Ruby SDK File Reference
pages.markdown:
# Ruby SDK File Reference

## upload (params, fileRoute, options)

Returns a JSON string.

Method used to upload file to the specified location on disk.

### **Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `params` | `ActionController::Parameters` | The request parameters, which hold the file that will be uploaded. |
| `fileRoute` | `String` | The path relative to the `Rails.root` global variable where the file should be uploaded. This parameter is optional, and defaults to `public/uploads/files`. |
| `options` | `Hash` | This parameter is optional. It can be used to pass custom options for the file upload. |

### **options parameter**

- **fieldname** The field name from the `params[:file]` global variable.  Type.StringDefault."file"
- **validation** A hash or a function used to validate the uploaded file. The hash's `allowedMimeTypes` list is not checked by the current gem, only `allowedExts`. The function is called with the file's path and mime type, and rejects the file by raising an exception.  Type.Hash or ProcDefault.validation: { allowedExts: [".txt", ".pdf", ".doc", ".json", ".html"], allowedMimeTypes: [ "text/plain", "application/msword", "application/x-pdf", "application/pdf", "application/json","text/html" ] }
- **file_access_path** The start of the link the method returns, followed by the new file name. Set it to the address where `fileRoute` is served.  Type.StringDefault."/uploads/"

### **Response**

If the upload is completed successfully, the method returns a JSON string with the link to the uploaded file, such as `{"link":"/uploads/files/abc.pdf"}`. If an error occurs, the method throws an exception.

```ruby
class UploadController < ActionController::Base

  ...

  def upload_file
    options = {
      fieldname: 'file',
      validation: {
        allowedExts: [".txt", ".pdf", ".doc", ".json", ".html"],
        allowedMimeTypes: [ "text/plain", "application/msword", "application/x-pdf", "application/pdf", "application/json","text/html" ]
      },
      file_access_path: '/uploads/files/'
    }
    render :json => FroalaEditorSDK::File.upload(params, "public/uploads/files/", options)
  end

  ...

end
```

## delete (file, path)

Returns a Boolean.

Method used to delete a file from disk.

### **Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `file` | `String` | The link of the file that should be deleted. Only its file name is used. |
| `path` | `String` | The path relative to the `Rails.root` global variable to the folder that holds the file. |

## data_hash (config)

Returns a Hash.

# Django File Upload ## File Upload The following sections describe how to handle file uploads on your server using Django as a server-side language. For information on the upload workflow refer to the [file upload documentation](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/concepts/file/upload/). ### *Frontend* Setting up the index page. 1. On the `head` section include the Editor style. 2. On the `body` section include the Editor JS files and define the area for the editor.

File upload example.

3. Initialize the editor and set the file upload URL The full code should look like this. ```html

File upload example.

``` ### *Backend* `views.py` handles the server part for django Inside views.py, the File class handles the file upload The code imports Wand, the Python binding for ImageMagick, so it needs both. Install Wand with pip and ImageMagick with your system's package manager. ```python from django.http import HttpResponse from django.conf import settings from django.shortcuts import render from os.path import isfile, join from mimetypes import MimeTypes from os import listdir from wand.image import Image import wand.image import hashlib import json import time import hmac import copy import sys import os def index(request): return render(request, os.path.join(settings.STATIC_DIR, "index.html")) def upload_file(request): options = { "validation": None } try: response = File.upload(DjangoAdapter(request), "/public/", options) except Exception: response = {"error": str(sys.exc_info()[1])} return HttpResponse(json.dumps(response), content_type="application/json") def upload_file_validation(request): def validation(filePath, mimetype): size = os.path.getsize(filePath) if size > 10 * 1024 * 1024: return False return True options = { "fieldname": "myFile", "validation": validation } try: response = File.upload(DjangoAdapter(request), "/public/", options) except Exception: response = {"error": str(sys.exc_info()[1])} return HttpResponse(json.dumps(response), content_type="application/json") class File(object): defaultUploadOptions = { "fieldname": "file", "validation": { "allowedExts": ["txt", "pdf", "doc"], "allowedMimeTypes": ["text/plain", "application/msword", "application/x-pdf", "application/pdf"] } } @staticmethod def upload(req, fileRoute, options = None): """ File upload to disk. Parameters: req: framework adapter to http request. See BaseAdapter. fileRoute: string options: dict optional, see defaultUploadOptions attribute Return: dict: {link: "linkPath"} """ if options is None: options = File.defaultUploadOptions else: options = Utils.merge_dicts(File.defaultUploadOptions, options) # Get extension. filename = req.getFilename(options["fieldname"]); extension = Utils.getExtension(filename) extension = "." + extension if extension else "" # Generate new random name. # python 2-3 compatible: try: sha1 = hashlib.sha1(str(time.time()).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest() # v3 except Exception: sha1 = hashlib.sha1(str(time.time())).hexdigest() # v2 routeFilename = fileRoute + sha1 + extension fullNamePath = Utils.getServerPath() + routeFilename req.saveFile(options["fieldname"], fullNamePath) # Check validation. if "validation" in options: if not Utils.isValid(options["validation"], fullNamePath, req.getMimetype(options["fieldname"])): File.delete(routeFilename) raise Exception("File does not meet the validation.") # Check image resize. if "resize" in options and options["resize"] is not None: with Image(filename=fullNamePath) as img: img.transform(resize=options["resize"]) img.save(filename=fullNamePath) # build and send response. response = {} response["link"] = routeFilename return response @staticmethod def delete(src): """ Delete file from disk. Parameters: src: string """ filePath = Utils.getServerPath() + src try: os.remove(filePath) except OSError: pass class Utils(object): """ Utils static class. """ @staticmethod def hmac(key, string, hex=False): """ Calculate hmac. Parameters: key: string string: string hex: boolean optional, return in hex, else return in binary Return: string: hmax in hex or binary """ # python 2-3 compatible: try: hmac256 = hmac.new(key.encode() if isinstance(key, str) else key, msg=string.encode("utf-8") if isinstance(string, str) else string, digestmod=hashlib.sha256) # v3 except Exception: hmac256 = hmac.new(key, msg=string, digestmod=hashlib.sha256) # v2 return hmac256.hexdigest() if hex else hmac256.digest() @staticmethod def merge_dicts(a, b, path=None): """ Deep merge two dicts without modifying them. Source: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/7204805/dictionaries-of-dictionaries-merge/7205107#7205107 Parameters: a: dict b: dict path: list Return: dict: Deep merged dict. """ aClone = copy.deepcopy(a); # Returns deep b into a without affecting the sources. if path is None: path = [] for key in b: if key in a: if isinstance(a[key], dict) and isinstance(b[key], dict): aClone[key] = Utils.merge_dicts(a[key], b[key], path + [str(key)]) else: aClone[key] = b[key] else: aClone[key] = b[key] return aClone @staticmethod def getExtension(filename): """ Get filename extension. Parameters: filename: string Return: string: The extension without the dot. """ return os.path.splitext(filename)[1][1:] @staticmethod def getServerPath(): """ Get the path where the server has started. Return: string: serverPath """ return os.path.abspath(os.path.dirname(sys.argv[0])) @staticmethod def isFileValid(filename, mimetype, allowedExts, allowedMimeTypes): """ Test if a file is valid based on its extension and mime type. Parameters: filename string mimeType string allowedExts list allowedMimeTypes list Return: boolean """ # Skip if the allowed extensions or mime types are missing. if not allowedExts or not allowedMimeTypes: return False extension = Utils.getExtension(filename) return extension.lower() in allowedExts and mimetype in allowedMimeTypes @staticmethod def isValid(validation, filePath, mimetype): """ Generic file validation. Parameters: validation: dict or function filePath: string mimetype: string """ # No validation means you dont want to validate, so return affirmative. if not validation: return True # Validation is a function provided by the user. if callable(validation): return validation(filePath, mimetype) if isinstance(validation, dict): return Utils.isFileValid(filePath, mimetype, validation["allowedExts"], validation["allowedMimeTypes"]) # Else: no specific validating behaviour found. return False class BaseAdapter(object): """ Interface. Inherit this class to use the lib in your framework. """ def __init__(self, request): """ Constructor. Parameters: request: http request object from some framework. """ self.request = request def riseError(self): """ Use this when you want to make an abstract method. """ raise NotImplementedError( "Should have implemented this method." ) def getFilename(self, fieldname): """ Get upload filename based on the fieldname. Parameters: fieldname: string Return: string: filename """ self.riseError() def getMimetype(self, fieldname): """ Get upload file mime type based on the fieldname. Parameters: fieldname: string Return: string: mimetype """ self.riseError() def saveFile(self, fieldname, fullNamePath): """ Save the upload file based on the fieldname on the fullNamePath location. Parameters: fieldname: string fullNamePath: string """ self.riseError() class DjangoAdapter(BaseAdapter): """ Django Adapter: Check BaseAdapter to see what methods description. """ def checkFile(self, fieldname): if fieldname not in self.request.FILES: raise Exception("File does not exist.") def getFilename(self, fieldname): self.checkFile(fieldname) return self.request.FILES[fieldname].name def getMimetype(self, fieldname): self.checkFile(fieldname) return self.request.FILES[fieldname].content_type def saveFile(self, fieldname, fullNamePath): print("should save now") print("the path" + fullNamePath) self.checkFile(fieldname) with open(fullNamePath, "wb+") as destination: for chunk in self.request.FILES[fieldname].chunks(): destination.write(chunk) ``` In `urls.py` define the request path with the according method, in this case the file upload. ```python from django.urls import re_path from . import views from django.conf.urls.static import static from django.conf import settings urlpatterns = [ re_path(r"^$", views.index, name="index"), re_path(r"^upload_file$", views.upload_file, name="upload_file"), re_path(r"^upload_file_validation", views.upload_file_validation, name="upload_file_validation"), ] + static(settings.STATIC_URL, document_root=settings.STATIC_DIR) + static(settings.STATIC_PUBLIC_URL, document_root=settings.STATIC_PUBLIC_DIR) ``` The code also reads three settings of its own. STATIC_DIR = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, "static") TEMPLATES[0]["DIRS"].append(STATIC_DIR) # The upload folder and its address. STATIC_PUBLIC_DIR = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, "public") STATIC_PUBLIC_URL = "/public/" os.makedirs(STATIC_PUBLIC_DIR, exist_ok=True) ``` ## Additional Resources - [Integrate Froala to Django Web Application with Image Upload](https://froala.com/blog/general/integrate-froala-to-django-web-application-with-image-upload/) - [What’s The Best Django WYSIWYG Editor With Image Upload?](https://froala.com/blog/editor/whats-the-best-django-wysiwyg-editor-with-image-upload/) - [6 Server Side Frameworks With WYSIWYG Editor Integration](https://froala.com/blog/general/6-server-side-frameworks-with-wysiwyg-editor-integration/)

# Ruby on Rails File Upload ## File Upload The following sections describe how to handle file uploads on your server using Ruby as a server-side language. For information on the upload workflow refer to the [file upload documentation](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/concepts/file/upload/). ### *Frontend* Setting up the index page. 1. On the `head` section include the Editor style. 2. On the `body` section include the Editor JS files and define the area for the editor.

File upload example.

3. Initialize the editor and set the file upload URL The full code should look like this. ```html

File upload example.

``` ### *Backend* `upload_controller.rb` handles the upload part. It has basic file format validations that can be easily extended. The uploads directory is created automatically if it does not exist under `public/uploads/files` If the uploaded file passes the validation step, the server responds with a JSON object containing a link to the uploaded file. For example, `{"link":"http://server_address/download_file/name_of_file"}`. ```ruby class UploadController < ActionController::Base # The editor's upload request does not carry the Rails CSRF token. skip_forgery_protection FILE_EXT = [".txt", ".pdf", ".doc"] def upload_file if params[:file] FileUtils::mkdir_p(Rails.root.join("public/uploads/files")) ext = File.extname(params[:file].original_filename) file_validation(ext) file_name = "#{SecureRandom.urlsafe_base64}#{ext}" path = Rails.root.join("public/uploads/files/", file_name) File.open(path, "wb") {|f| f.write(params[:file].read)} view_file = Rails.root.join("/download_file/", file_name).to_s render :json => {:link => view_file}.to_json else render :json => {:link => nil}.to_json end end def file_validation(ext) raise "Not allowed" unless FILE_EXT.include?(ext) end def access_file if File.exist?(Rails.root.join("public", "uploads", "files", params[:name])) send_data File.read(Rails.root.join("public", "uploads", "files", params[:name])), :disposition => "attachment" else head :not_found end end end ``` `routes.rb` handles the routing part. Inside this file you need to define the routes for the POST file upload and the GET uploaded file requests ```ruby Rails.application.routes.draw do # For details on the DSL available within this file, see http://guides.rubyonrails.org/routing.html post "/upload_file" => "upload#upload_file", :as => :upload_file get "/download_file/:name" => "upload#access_file", :as => :upload_access_file, :name => /.*/ end ```

For example, `{"link":"http://server_address/download_file/name_of_file"}`. ```ruby class UploadController < ActionController::Base # The editor's upload request does not carry the Rails CSRF token. skip_forgery_protection IMAGE_EXT = [".gif", ".jpeg", ".jpg", ".png", ".svg"] def upload_image if params[:file] FileUtils::mkdir_p(Rails.root.join("public/uploads/files")) ext = File.extname(params[:file].original_filename) image_validation(ext) file_name = "#{SecureRandom.urlsafe_base64}#{ext}" path = Rails.root.join("public/uploads/files/", file_name) File.open(path, "wb") {|f| f.write(params[:file].read)} view_file = Rails.root.join("/download_file/", file_name).to_s render :json => {:link => view_file}.to_json else render :json => {:link => nil}.to_json end end def image_validation(ext) raise "Not allowed" unless IMAGE_EXT.include?(ext) end def access_file if File.exist?(Rails.root.join("public", "uploads", "files", params[:name])) send_data File.read(Rails.root.join("public", "uploads", "files", params[:name])), :disposition => "attachment" else head :not_found end end end ``` `routes.rb` handles the routing part. Inside this file you need to define the routes for the POST image upload and the GET uploaded image requests ```ruby Rails.application.routes.draw do # For details on the DSL available within this file, see http://guides.rubyonrails.org/routing.html post "/upload_image" => "upload#upload_image", :as => :upload_image get "/download_file/:name" => "upload#access_file", :as => :upload_access_file, :name => /.*/ end ```

# AI Assist - Direct OpenAI API Integration ## AI Assist ### Use AI Assist with a Direct API Call (Fast Frontend Setup for Prototyping) This example shows how to connect AI Assist plugin directly to an AI API from the frontend, without setting up a backend, so you can prototype in minutes. ### In This Example The AI Assist plugin is model-agnostic, offering the flexibility to integrate with any AI API and choose the provider that best fits your needs and budget. In this example, you’ll learn how to setup AI Assist with OpenAI: - Uses `aiAssistRequest` to directly call the **OpenAI Chat Completions API**. - Sends user prompt + an initial system instruction. - Specifies model (gpt-4), max tokens, and temperature. - Returns the generated HTML content to be inserted into the editor. ### Before You Start This approach is designed for **prototyping and experimentation**. Since API calls are made directly from the frontend: - Your API key is exposed in the client - Responses are not validated server-side - There’s limited control over usage and logging For production apps, use a [backend integration](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/examples/ai-assist-custom-backend-with-validation-event-hooks/) instead. ### Key Points:  ✔ Fully client-side ✔ Uses fetch to call OpenAI’s API ✔ Requires the developer to provide their own API key ✦ May expose API key if used in front-end code → should ideally be proxied via backend #### HTML ```
``` #### JAVASCRIPT ``` ``` ### How It Works The flow is straightforward: 1. User triggers AI Assist in the editor 2. A request is sent directly to the AI API 3. The response is returned to the browser 4. Content is inserted into the editor No backend required, just a direct connection. ### When to Use This Approach This setup is ideal if you’re: - Prototyping AI feature. - Testing prompts and UX flows - Building demos or proofs of concept - Exploring how AI Assist fits your product If your goal is **speed over control**, this is the right approach. For production apps, use a [backend integration](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/examples/ai-assist-custom-backend-with-validation-event-hooks/) instead. ### Try AI Assist feature yourself: Try AI Assist in our [overview demo.](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/demo/) ## Additional Resources - [How to Set Up Froala with DeepSeek AI Assist in WordPress](https://froala.com/blog/editor/tutorials/froala-deepseek-ai-wordpress-setup/) - [Introduce AI Assist Plugin](https://froala.com/blog/editor/new-releases/froala-5-1-release-ai-assist-plugin/)

pages.markdown:
# Codox Real-time Editing

## Codox Real-time Editing

Froala WYSIWYG HTML Editor has an official plugin and [integration for real-time](https://froala.com/blog/editor/top-6-amazing-advantages-of-real-time-html-editors/?amp=1) collaboration with Codox.io

The value of `apiKeyin` the query string should be set to the one created for your Froala integration on the dashboard:

  

### How it works:

Add the following JavaScript block to your application to enable real-time co-editing for Froala. Replace the apiKey field with your own, which you can get [here.](https://app.codox.io/)

The co-editing session will start inside the Froala editor instance specified in the `editor` attribute.

Before invoking `codox.init()` the Froala editor should be fully initialized. In the example code, we ensure that Froala is initialized first by adding an `initialized` [event hook](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/events#initialized) to Froala's constructor.

The values for `docId` and `username` should come from your document management service. Wave expects `docId` to be globally unique across your service.

#### CSS

```
<!-- Include the following css file. -->
<link href="https://cdn1.codox.io/lib/css/wave.client.css" rel="stylesheet">
```

#### JAVASCRIPT

```
<!-- Include the following js file. -->
<script src="https://app.codox.io/plugins/wave.client.js?apiKey=your-api-key&app=froala" type="text/javascript"></script>
<script>
  const codox = new Codox();
  const editor = new FroalaEditor('#editor', {
      events: {
        //setting up on initialization event
        'initialized': function() {
          //Adding Wave configuration
          var config = { 
            "app"      : "froala",
            "docId"    : "mydoc",
            "username" : "Chris",
            "editor"   : editor,
            "apiKey"   : "d5bb1f48-356b-4032-8d0c-ba1a79396f79", //replace this
          };  
          
          codox.init(config);
      }   
  }
</script>
```

## Demo #1

### How to test

Start editing in one editor and the edits will appear on both editors. This represents you are editing content and your edits appear to your co-worker on his own editor.

## Demo #2

### Overview

This demo starting by displaying "Demo will load shortly" message which will be replaced with a Froala editor with at least one avatar above the top-right corner of the editor window. Each avatar is representing a user (on of them is You) who joins a co-editing session. Avatars will have a random name just for testing purposes.

If there are more than one avatars, it means there are other users opening this page at the same time.

The max number of avatars is three which is determined based on our subscription plan with codox.io.

If the "Demo will load shortly". message is replaced with 'The real-time collaboration demo will not work because the number of users exceeds the allowed number of users/session in the codox.io plan we subscribed to, Wait a little until one of the users leaves the page.' message, this means there are three or more users currently testing this demo, you could wait on the page and once a user leaves, the demo will start automatically.

  

### How to test

-   Open this page on two different browser windows.
-   Minimize the browser windows and make them aligned horizontally.
-   You should now have a Froala editor opened on each page.
-   Start typing on one editor and you should be able to see the changes are displayed in [real-time on the other editor](https://froala.com/blog/editor/top-6-amazing-advantages-of-real-time-html-editors/?amp=1) with the name of the editor.

pages.title: Font Family Options in Froala Editor
pages.markdown:
# Font Family Options in Froala Editor ## Font Family When using the `font_family.min.js` plugin it is possible to add your own fonts to be used inside the WYSIWYG HTML editor. ### Try it yourself: First you have to include the font on your webpage. In this example we are adding 4 Google fonts: Roboto, Oswald, Montserrat and Open Sans Condensed. Then you have to define the fonts that should appear in the Font Family dropdown using the [fontFamily](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/options#fontFamily "fontFamily") option. This option is an Object where the key represents the font name (just the way you would pass it to the `font-family` CSS rule e.g. `font-family: **'Roboto', sans-serif**;`) and its value is the font name that appears in the dropdown list e.g. `**Roboto**`. [Edit in JSFiddle](https://jsfiddle.net/Froala_marketing/o20akxgw/ "Edit Font Family in JSFiddle") #### HTML ```

By default the font family icon is visible in the editor's toolbar. If you want to be able to see the actual font family for the selected text you can use the fontFamilySelection option.

``` #### CSS ``` ``` #### JAVASCRIPT ``` ``` Related Plugin: [Font Family](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/plugins/font-family-plugin/)

pages.markdown:
# Languages The editor's interface is in English (United States) by default. The package ships 39 language files to change it. ## Set the Language Load the language file after the editor, then set the `language` option to its code. The examples below switch the editor to Spanish (`es`). ### In an HTML Page ```html
``` ### In a JavaScript Module ```js import FroalaEditor from 'froala-editor'; import 'froala-editor/js/languages/es.js'; new FroalaEditor('#editor', { language: 'es' }); ``` React, Vue and Angular import the file the same way and pass `language` with the other options. See the [React guide](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/framework-plugins/react/) for an example. ## Available Languages | Language | Code | | --- | --- | | Arabic | `ar` | | Bosnian | `bs` | | Chinese (China) | `zh_cn` | | Chinese (Taiwan) | `zh_tw` | | Croatian | `hr` | | Czech | `cs` | | Danish | `da` | | Dutch | `nl` | | English (Canada) | `en_ca` | | English (United Kingdom) | `en_gb` | | Estonian | `et` | | Finnish | `fi` | | French | `fr` | | German | `de` | | Greek | `el` | | Hebrew | `he` | | Hungarian | `hu` | | Indonesian | `id` | | Italian | `it` | | Japanese | `ja` | | Korean | `ko` | | Kurdish | `ku` | | Montenegrin | `me` | | Norwegian | `nb` | | Persian | `fa` | | Polish | `pl` | | Portuguese (Brazil) | `pt_br` | | Portuguese (Portugal) | `pt_pt` | | Romanian | `ro` | | Russian | `ru` | | Serbian | `sr` | | Slovak | `sk` | | Slovenian | `sl` | | Spanish | `es` | | Swedish | `sv` | | Thai | `th` | | Turkish | `tr` | | Ukrainian | `uk` | | Vietnamese | `vi` | The file for each language is `js/languages/.js`. English (United States) is built in and has no file. ## Right to Left The Arabic, Hebrew, Kurdish and Persian files turn the whole editor right to left, toolbar included. A language file's direction replaces the `direction` option. For any other language, set `direction` yourself. It takes `'auto'` (the default), `'ltr'` or `'rtl'`. With `'auto'`, only the text in the editing area follows the typing direction and the toolbar stays as it is. ```js new FroalaEditor('#editor', { direction: 'rtl' }); ``` ## Add or Change a Language A language file adds its strings to `FroalaEditor.LANGUAGE` under its code, keyed by the English text. Register your own the same way, after the editor script. Strings it leaves out stay in English. ```js FroalaEditor.LANGUAGE['xx'] = { translation: { 'Bold': 'Your word for Bold', 'Italic': 'Your word for Italic' }, direction: 'ltr' }; new FroalaEditor('#editor', { language: 'xx' }); ``` To fix a translation or suggest a new language, [contact us](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/contact/). ## Additional Resources - [Language example](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/examples/language/) - [Creating React Rich Text Editor for Right-to-Left Languages](https://froala.com/blog/editor/tutorials/creating-react-rich-text-editor-for-right-to-left-languages/) - [Add Multilingual Translation to Froala with Translate Plus API from APILayer](https://froala.com/blog/editor/how-to-easily-add-multilingual-translation-to-your-froala-editor/)

pages.title: Shortcuts
pages.markdown:
# Shortcuts

`Ctrl` on Windows and Linux is `⌘ Cmd` on a Mac. A shortcut works when the plugin in its row is loaded; Core ones come with the editor, and Browser ones are the browser's own.

## Inline Editor

| Action | Windows and Linux | Mac | Plugin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Show the inline toolbar | `Ctrl` + `E` | `⌘ Cmd` + `E` | Core |

This works when `toolbarInline` is `true`.

## Common Actions

| Action | Windows and Linux | Mac | Plugin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Copy | `Ctrl` + `C` | `⌘ Cmd` + `C` | Browser |
| Cut | `Ctrl` + `X` | `⌘ Cmd` + `X` | Browser |
| Paste | `Ctrl` + `V` | `⌘ Cmd` + `V` | Browser |
| Undo | `Ctrl` + `Z` | `⌘ Cmd` + `Z` | Core |
| Redo | `Ctrl` + `Y` or `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `Z` | `⌘ Cmd` + `⇧ Shift` + `Z` or `⌘ Cmd` + `Y` | Core |
| Open the insert link popup | `Ctrl` + `K` | `⌘ Cmd` + `K` | Link |
| Open the insert image popup | `Ctrl` + `P` | `⌘ Cmd` + `P` | Image |
| Insert an anchor | `Ctrl` + `D` | `⌘ Cmd` + `D` | Anchor |
| Find and replace | `Ctrl` + `F` | `⌘ Cmd` + `F` | Find and Replace |

The Image and Files Manager plugins both claim `Ctrl` + `P`, and the one loaded last wins. With `plugins.pkgd.min.js` that is Image. With Files Manager alone, the keys open Insert Files.

## Basic Formatting

| Action | Windows and Linux | Mac | Plugin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Select all | `Ctrl` + `A` | `⌘ Cmd` + `A` | Browser |
| Bold | `Ctrl` + `B` | `⌘ Cmd` + `B` | Core |
| Italic | `Ctrl` + `I` | `⌘ Cmd` + `I` | Core |
| Underline | `Ctrl` + `U` | `⌘ Cmd` + `U` | Core |
| Strikethrough | `Ctrl` + `S` | `⌘ Cmd` + `S` | Core |
| Indent the paragraph | `Ctrl` + `]` | `⌘ Cmd` + `]` | Core |
| Outdent the paragraph | `Ctrl` + `[` | `⌘ Cmd` + `[` | Core |

## Quote

| Action | Windows and Linux | Mac | Plugin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Increase the quote level | `Ctrl` + `'` | `⌘ Cmd` + `'` | Quote |
| Decrease the quote level | `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `'` | `⌘ Cmd` + `⇧ Shift` + `'` | Quote |

## Image and Video

| Action | Windows and Linux | Mac | Plugin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Make the image or video larger | `Ctrl` + `+` | `⌘ Cmd` + `+` | Image, Video |
| Make the image or video smaller | `Ctrl` + `-` | `⌘ Cmd` + `-` | Image, Video |

Select the image or video first.

## Table

| Action | Windows and Linux | Mac | Plugin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Select the cell the cursor is in | `Alt` + `Space` | `⌥ Option` + `Space` | Table |
| Extend the selection one cell left or right | `Shift` + `Left` or `Shift` + `Right` | `⇧ Shift` + `Left` or `⇧ Shift` + `Right` | Table |
| Extend the selection one row up or down | `Shift` + `Up` or `Shift` + `Down` | `⇧ Shift` + `Up` or `⇧ Shift` + `Down` | Table |

Put the cursor in a cell first. The arrow keys extend the selection once a cell is selected.

## Navigation

| Action | Windows and Linux | Mac | Plugin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Show the list of shortcuts | `Ctrl` + `/` | `⌘ Cmd` + `/` | Help |
| Move focus to the open popup or the toolbar | `Alt` + `F10` | `⌥ Option` + `F10` | Core |
| Return focus to where it was | `Esc` | `Esc` | Core |

## AI and Comments

| Action | Windows and Linux | Mac | Plugin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Open AI Assist | `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `I` | `⌘ Cmd` + `⇧ Shift` + `I` | AI Assist |
| Add a comment | `Ctrl` + `M` | `⌘ Cmd` + `M` | Collaborative |

## Change the Shortcuts

| Option or event | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `shortcutsEnabled` | The commands whose shortcuts work. By default, every shortcut the loaded plugins register. |
| `shortcutsHint` | Shows the shortcut in the toolbar button's tooltip. On by default. |
| `shortcut` event | Runs before a shortcut's command, with the event, the command name and its value. Return `false` to stop the command. |

```js
new FroalaEditor('#editor', {
  // Keep only these two shortcuts.
  shortcutsEnabled: ['bold', 'italic'],
  events: {
    shortcut: function (e, cmd, val) {
      console.log(cmd, val);
    }
  }
});
```

### Add a Shortcut

Register it with `FroalaEditor.RegisterShortcut` before the editor starts. This one turns the paragraph into a Heading 1 with `Ctrl` + `1`.

```js
// RegisterShortcut(keyCode, command, value, letter, shiftKey, optionKey)
FroalaEditor.RegisterShortcut(49, 'paragraphFormat', 'H1', 'H', false);
```

| Argument | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `keyCode` | The key code of the key, such as `49` for 1. |
| `command` | The command to run. |
| `value` | The value passed to the command. Optional. |
| `letter` | The key shown in the tooltip. Optional. |
| `shiftKey` | Whether `Shift` must be held too. Optional. |
| `optionKey` | Whether `Alt` (`⌥ Option`) must be held too. Optional. |

- [Shortcuts example](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/examples/shortcuts/)
- [Custom shortcut](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/concepts/custom/shortcut/)
- [Help plugin](https://froala.com/wysiwyg-editor/docs/plugins/help-plugin/)
